title: The same act can spring from different doctrines
source_text: Καὶ πρὸς ταῦτα δὲ λεκτέον ὅτι, εἴπερ Σκύθαι καὶ Λιβύων οἱ Νομάδες καὶ Σῆρες, οὕς φησιν ἀθέους εἶναι ὁ Κέλσος. καὶ ἄλλα ἔθνη δυσαγέστατα καὶ ἀνομώτατα ἀλλὰ καὶ Πέρσαι οὐκ ἀνέχονται νεὼς ὁρῶντες καὶ βωμοὺς καὶ ἀγάλματα, οὐ παρὰ τοῦτο ἴσον ἐστὶ τὸ μὴ ἀνέχεσθαι τούτων ἐκείνους τῷ καὶ ἡμᾶς μὴ ἀνέχεσθαι αὐτῶν. ἐξεταστέον γὰρ τὰ δόγματα, ἀφ᾿ ὧν ὁρμώμενοι οὐκ ἀνέχονται ναῶν καὶ ἀγαλμάτων οἱ μὴ ἀνεχόμενοί γε αὐτῶν· ἵν᾿, εἰ μὲν ἀπὸ ὑγιῶν δογμάτων οὐκ ἀνέχεται. ἐπαινῆται ὁ μὴ ἀνεχόμενος, εἰ δ᾿ ἀπὸ ἐσφαλμένων, ψέγηται. δυνατὸν γὰρ τὸ αὐτὸ ἀπὸ διαφόρων δογμάτων γίνεσθαι. οἷον ἐπὶ παραδείγματος ἐκκλίνουσι τὸ μοιχεύειν οἱ τὰ τοῦ Κιτιέως Ζήνωνος φιλοσοφοῦντες ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ τὰ Ἐπικούρου τινὲς δὲ καὶ τῶν παντελῶς ἰδιωτῶν. ἀλλ᾿ ὅρα ὅση διαφωνία ἐστὶ περὶ τῆς τοῦ μοιχεύειν ἐκκλίσεως τῶν τοσούτων· οἱ μὲν διὰ τὸ κοινωνικὸν καὶ παρὰ φύσιν εἶναι τῷ λογικῷ ζῴῳ νοθεύειν τὴν ὑπὸ τῶν νόμων ἑτέρῳ προκαταληφθεῖσαν γυναῖκα καὶ φθείρειν τὸν ἄλλου ἀνθρώπου οἶκον, οἱ δὲ ἀπὸ Ἐπικούρου οὐ διὰ τοῦτο οὐ μοιχεύουσιν, ὅτε ἀπέχονται τοῦ μοιχεύειν. ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸ νενομικέναι τέλος τὴν ἡδονὴν, πολλὰ δ᾿ ἀπαντᾶν κωλυτικὰ τῆς ἡδονῆς τῷ εἴξαντι μιᾷ τῇ τοῦ μοιχεύειν ἡδονῇ καὶ ἔσθ᾿ ὅτε φυλακὰς ἢ θανάτους πολλάκις δὲ πρὸ τούτων καὶ κινδύνους κατὰ τὸ ἐπιτηρεῖν τὴν τοῦ ἀνδρὸς ἔξοδον ἀπὸ τῆς οἰκίας καὶ τῶν τὰ ἐκείνου φρονούντων· ὡς εἰ καθ᾿ ὑπόθεσιν μοιχεύοντα οἷόν τ᾿ ἦν λαθεῖν καὶ τὸν ἄνδρα τῆς γυναικὸς καὶ τοὺς οἰκείους πάντας αὐτοῦ καὶ τοὺς, παρ᾿ οἷς τις ἐκ τοῦ μοιχεύειν χεύειν ἀδοξεῖ. κἂν ἐμοίχευσε διὰ τὴν ἡδονὴν ὁ Ἐπικούρειος. εἰ δὲ καὶ ὁ ἰδιώτης ποτὲ παρὸν μοιχεύειν οὐ μοιχεύει, εὑρεθείη ἂν ἐνίοτε διὰ τὸν ἐνεστῶτα ἐκ τοῦ νόμου φόβον καὶ τὰς κολάσεις (οὐ) μοιχεύων. καὶ οὐ διὰ τὸ θηρᾶσθαι πλείονας ἡδονὰς ὁ τοιοῦτος ἀπέχοιτ᾿ ἂν τοῦ μοιχεύειν. ὁρᾷς οὖν ὅτι τὸ ἓν εἶναι νομιζόμενον ἔργον. ἡ τῆς μοιχείας ἀποχὴ, παρὰ τὰς προθέσεις τῶν ἀπεχομένων οὐ ταὐτὸν ἀλλὰ διάφορον γίνεται· ἢ γὰρ ἀπὸ ὑγιῶν δογμάτων ἢ ἀπὸ μοχθηρῶν καὶ ἀσεβεστάτων τῶν ἐν τῷ Ἐπικουρείῳ ἢ τῷ τοιῷδε ἰδιώτῃ.
pass_a_gloss: And to these it must be said that, if Scythians and the Nomads of the Libyans and Seres, whom Celsus says to be godless (ἄθεοι), and other most unholy and lawless nations, but also Persians, do not endure (ἀνέχομαι) seeing temples and altars and images, not on this account (παρὰ τοῦτο) is their not enduring these equal (ἴσος) to our also not enduring them. For one must examine (ἐξεταστέον) the doctrines (δόγματα) from which, setting out (ὁρμάομαι), those not enduring temples and images do not endure them; so that, if from sound (ὑγιής) doctrines he does not endure, the one not enduring may be praised (ἐπαινέω), but if from erring (σφάλλω) ones, blamed (ψέγω). For it is possible for the same thing to come about from different (διάφορα) doctrines. As for example, those philosophizing the things of Zeno of Citium avoid (ἐκκλίνω) committing adultery (μοιχεύω), but also those of Epicurus, and some even of the wholly unlearned (ἰδιῶται). But see how much disagreement (διαφωνία) there is about the avoidance (ἔκκλισις) of adultery among so many: some on account of the social (τὸ κοινωνικόν) and its being against nature (παρὰ φύσιν) for the rational being (λογικὸν ζῷον) to corrupt (νοθεύω) the woman taken beforehand (προκαταλαμβάνω) by the laws for another and to ruin (φθείρω) another man's house (οἶκος); but those from Epicurus do not on this account not commit adultery, when they abstain (ἀπέχομαι) from adultery, but on account of having held (νομίζω) pleasure (ἡδονή) the end (τέλος), and many things hindering (κωλυτικά) pleasure meeting the one who yields (εἴκω) to the one pleasure of adultery, and sometimes prisons (φυλακαί) or deaths, and often before these also dangers (κίνδυνοι) in watching (ἐπιτηρέω) the going out (ἔξοδος) from the house of the husband and of those minded as he (τὰ ἐκείνου φρονοῦντες); so that if by hypothesis (καθ᾿ ὑπόθεσιν) it were possible for one committing adultery to escape the notice (λανθάνω) of the woman's husband and all his household and those among whom one is in ill repute (ἀδοξέω) from adultery, the Epicurean would have committed adultery for the pleasure. And if the ordinary man too sometimes, it being possible to commit adultery, does not commit adultery, he would be found at times, on account of the present (ἐνεστώς) fear (φόβος) from the law and the punishments (κολάσεις), <not> committing adultery; and not on account of hunting (θηράομαι) more pleasures would such a one abstain from adultery. You see then that the work (ἔργον) thought to be one, the abstinence (ἀποχή) from adultery, becomes, according to the purposes (προθέσεις) of those abstaining, not the same but different; for [it is] either from sound doctrines or from wicked (μοχθηρά) and most impious (ἀσεβέστατα) ones, those in the Epicurean or in such an ordinary man.
pass_b_english: To this too we must say that, if the Scythians and the Nomads of Libya and the Seres, whom Celsus calls godless, and other most unholy and lawless nations, and the Persians as well, cannot bear the sight of temples and altars and images, their refusal to bear these things is not, on that account, the same as our refusal to bear them. For we must examine the doctrines that move those who cannot bear temples and images to refuse them, so that one who refuses them on the basis of sound doctrines may be praised, and one who refuses them on the basis of mistaken ones may be blamed. For the same act can come about from different doctrines.

For example, those who pursue the philosophy of Zeno of Citium shun adultery, but so do the followers of Epicurus, and so do some who are wholly unlearned. But see how great a disagreement there is among so many people about why they shun adultery. Some shun it out of regard for the common good, and because it is against nature for a rational being to corrupt a woman whom the laws have already secured to another, and to ruin another man’s household. But the followers of Epicurus, when they abstain from adultery, do not refrain for this reason; they refrain because they hold pleasure to be the end, and because many things that hinder pleasure meet the man who yields to the single pleasure of adultery: sometimes imprisonment or death, and often, before these, dangers too, in watching for the husband, and those who take his side, to go out of the house. So if, by hypothesis, a man committing adultery could escape the notice of the woman’s husband, and of all his household, and of those in whose eyes a man loses his good name through adultery, the Epicurean would even have committed adultery for the sake of pleasure.

And if the unlearned man too, at some time when he could commit adultery, does not commit it, he would sometimes be found refraining from adultery because of the fear that the law holds over him and its punishments; and it would not be in pursuit of greater pleasures that such a man abstained from adultery. You see, then, that what is thought to be one act, abstaining from adultery, is not the same but different according to the purposes of those who abstain; for it comes either from sound doctrines, or from the wicked and most impious ones held by the Epicurean, or by such an unlearned man.

choices.choice: Origen restates Celsus’s list from 7.62 in indirect speech, so no quotation marks are used. ‘μοιχεύειν χεύειν’ in the staged text is a dittography; read once. Koetschau’s supplement (οὐ) before μοιχεύων accepted; the sense requires it. οἱ μέν (‘some’) are Zeno’s followers, the Stoics, though Origen does not name them again. τὸ κοινωνικόν: ‘the common good’ (human fellowship, a Stoic term). τέλος: ‘the end’, the Epicurean goal of life. φυλακάς: ‘imprisonment’. τῶν τὰ ἐκείνου φρονούντων: ‘those who take his side’. νοθεύειν: ‘to corrupt’ (literally to make spurious). προκαταληφθεῖσαν: ‘already secured to another’ by the laws, that is, already married. κἂν ἐμοίχευσε: ‘would even have committed adultery’. The final clause groups the Epicurean and the unlearned man together under ‘wicked and most impious’ doctrines as the Greek does. No Scripture quoted.
οὐ παρὰ τοῦτο ἴσον ἐστί: 'it does not follow from this that their not bearing ... is equal to' -> 'their refusal ... is not, on that account, the same as our refusal'

ἀφ᾿ ὧν ὁρμώμενοι ... ἵν᾿ ... ἐπαινῆται ... ψέγηται: stiff Greek order recast ('the doctrines that move those who cannot bear temples and images to refuse them, so that one who refuses them on the basis of sound doctrines may be praised ...')
τινὲς δὲ καὶ τῶν παντελῶς ἰδιωτῶν: 'some even of the wholly unlearned' -> 'so do some who are wholly unlearned'
μοιχεύοντα ... λαθεῖν: 'the adulterer' -> 'a man committing adultery'; κἄν: 'would even have committed'
οὐ διὰ τὸ θηρᾶσθαι πλείονας ἡδονάς: contrast with the Epicurean made clear ('it would not be in pursuit of greater pleasures that such a man abstained')
τῶν ἐν τῷ Ἐπικουρείῳ: added 'such as those found in' -> 'held by'
